source.title: Scaling Laws for EEG Decoding: How Much Data Is Enough?
source.citation: José Manuel Nunes de Oliveira et al., 2026
source.authors: José Manuel Nunes de Oliveira; Bruna J. Lopes; Léo Burgund; Raphael Y. Camargo; B. Aristimunha

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends power-law scaling analysis to EEG decoding and reports fitted loss curves and held-out prediction errors for that modality.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports CTNet balanced-accuracy comparisons across matched-volume data allocations (Fig. 3). Those results compare allocations but do not test whether loss follows a power law, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits a Hoffmann-style additive power law (trials per subject, number of subjects) to held-out test cross-entropy loss of five supervised EEG decoders on four datasets. It then checks predictions at held-out subject fractions. This is a new modality and regime (EEG classification, data-volume scaling only), so it bears on V5. It is not one of V5's original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that EEG decoding loss scales with data and that power laws are a useful descriptive framework within the tested conditions. The fitted parameters are model- and dataset-specific, and most fits extrapolate to larger subject pools with RMSE below 0.1. They add that the trial-versus-subject distinction becomes largely irrelevant as total volume grows, and that subject diversity is the binding constraint for data acquisition.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits EEG test loss against training trials per subject and number of subjects, rather than language-model loss against parameters, tokens, or compute. The repo/code used for the experiments is not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling parameters vary across models and datasets; EEGNeX shows no apparent data-volume scaling on ISRUC. The authors also report a general difference between trial- and subject-scaling contributions across dataset/model pairs.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched data volume, CTNet balanced accuracy differs little between subject-heavy, trial-heavy and balanced allocations. Accuracy does differ across volume tiers. The exception is PhysioNet Low, where trial-heavy is worse than balanced (Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In supervised EEG decoding, total data volume matters more than how data are split between subjects and per-subject recording time.

fits_no_version.finding: A relative trial-versus-subject contribution measure varies by dataset: trials dominate on ISRUC, subjects on TUAB and NMT (Fig. 2). The authors conclude subject diversity is the binding constraint.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which data dimension drives EEG loss scaling depends on the dataset and task.

record.problems: The study covers EEG decoding rather than language models, and tests data-volume scaling rather than parameter or compute scaling. Results are specific to the tested architectures, tasks, and datasets; the authors note that architectural heterogeneity prevents isolating model-size effects. Table 2 does not report uncertainty for fitted parameters or RMSE, although the paper says each condition was repeated with five seeds and Fig. 1 shows ±1 seed SD.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3's CTNet balanced-accuracy results compare data compositions at matched volumes rather than testing power-law test-loss fits, so they were not entered as rows.

untested.parts: Image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. Model-size or compute scaling in EEG: the authors say architectural heterogeneity prevents isolating model size. Scaling over several orders of magnitude: subjects span only 10–100% (about one decade) and extrapolation is only from ≤50% to 75–100%.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested: there is no language-model extrapolation, and the EEG extrapolation is only about 2x, not orders of magnitude.
Not tested: no compute-budget allocation between parameters and tokens.
Not tested: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Not tested: no language-model downstream tasks.
Not tested for language-model laws. EEG exponents vary by model and dataset, but these are not language-model fitting-choice comparisons.

missing.what: Saturation thresholds where extra per-subject trials give negligible loss gains once enough subjects are present (e.g. PhysioNet ~65 subjects and ~70% of trials; TUAB and NMT 90–92% of gain at 40% of trials)
Seed variability (±1 SD over five seeds) of test loss shown in Fig. 1; Table 2 gives no uncertainty for fitted parameters or RMSE

record.verdict_notes: Setting: supervised EEG classifiers trained for 100 epochs. Measure: test cross-entropy at the best-validation epoch. Only data volume is scaled, not model size or compute. The 'extrapolation' is modest, at most 2–10x within one decade of subjects, so these results do not show multi-order-of-magnitude power laws. RMSE is in absolute loss units, and the 0.1 threshold is the authors' benchmark. Several fits have degenerate parameters (amplitudes in the thousands, exponents near 2–2.5) or zero trial terms, which weakens reading the fitted exponents as meaningful.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests EEG decoding, not held-out pretraining loss of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
The study predicts EEG loss at held-out subject fractions, but does not test language-model runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitted runs.
It does not vary language-model parameters and training tokens under a fixed compute budget or estimate a compute-optimal split.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests EEG decoding, but not image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
It does not study downstream task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.

The study reports model- and dataset-specific EEG scaling fits, but does not test language-model fitting choices, disagreement between published language-model laws, compute-optimal splits, or bending of language-model curves.

relationships.condition: EEG decoders where both trial and subject terms scale and held-out RMSE ≤0.09 (PhysioNet ATCNet/EEGNeX/MSVTNet/REVE; ISRUC ATCNet/CTNet/MSVTNet/REVE; TUAB ATCNet/EEGNeX/MSVTNet/REVE; NMT ATCNet)
relationships.reason: Additive power-law fits on 10–50% of subjects predict 75–100% subject losses with RMSE 0.01–0.09 (R1, R3–R7, R9–R11, R13–R16). The range covered is only about one decade.
relationships.display_finding: Fits using 10–50% of subjects predicted losses at 75–100% of subjects with RMSE of 0.01–0.09, across approximately one decade of scaling.

source_check.reason: R1, R3–R7, R9–R11 and R13–R16 report positive exponents for both dimensions and held-out RMSE 0.01–0.09, supporting the descriptive power-law form within the tested range.

relationships.reason: Held-out RMSE is 0.15 and 0.11, above the authors' 0.1 benchmark, so the fit predicts held-out subject losses less well (R2, R12).
relationships.display_finding: Held-out RMSEs were 0.15 and 0.11, exceeding the authors' 0.1 benchmark for predicting subject losses.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R2 and R12 report held-out RMSE 0.15 and 0.11, indicating weaker predictive agreement than the other successful fits; this qualifies predictive applicability without establishing absent scaling.

relationships.reason: Fitted trial exponents are 0.00–0.01, so loss does not scale with trials per subject; only weak subject scaling remains (R17–R20).
relationships.display_finding: Trial exponents were 0.00–0.01, indicating negligible improvement from more trials per subject and only weak scaling with subjects.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R17–R20 report trial exponents 0.00, 0.00, 0.00 and 0.01, respectively, while subject exponents remain positive. Scaling is therefore restricted mainly to subject count; REVE's trial dependence is nearly flat rather than exactly absent.

relationships.reason: The authors state EEGNeX showed no apparent scaling with data volume on ISRUC. Its fit is degenerate (A=4.7k, α=2.47) with held-out RMSE=0.30 (R8).
relationships.display_finding: Performance showed no apparent improvement with data volume, and the degenerate fit had A=4.7k, α=2.47 and held-out RMSE=0.30.
